pharm: Long-acting, non-sedating peripheral H1-receptor antagonist withdrawn worldwide because of dose- and exposure-dependent QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.
quick: Historical: 10 mg once daily (no longer used - withdrawn)
Take on empty stomach; bioavailability reduced by food
Contraindicated/avoid - impaired clearance raises cardiotoxicity risk
ECG/QT was required - drug withdrawn for cardiotoxicity
summary: Astemizole is a long-acting, non-sedating second-generation H1-antihistamine formerly used for allergic rhinitis and chronic urticaria at 10 mg once daily. It was withdrawn from markets worldwide (and its US approval discontinued) after reports of QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, cardiac arrest and death, especially at higher-than-recommended doses, in overdose, in hepatic impairment, or when combined with CYP3A4 inhibitors. It is no longer recommended for use and is not an FDA-approved agent in current practice.
indications: Historical: symptomatic relief of seasonal and perennial allergic rhinitis (no longer used)
Historical: chronic idiopathic urticaria (no longer used)
Note: all indications superseded by safer second-generation antihistamines following worldwide withdrawal

dosage.n: WITHDRAWN - exceeding 10 mg/day markedly increased fatal arrhythmia risk; dose should never have been increased to hasten onset
Historical only; no longer used owing to cardiotoxicity
Drug withdrawn worldwide for QT prolongation / torsades; use a safer second-generation antihistamine instead

admin: Was taken once daily on an empty stomach (at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals) as food reduced absorption
The recommended dose was never to be exceeded - higher doses caused life-threatening arrhythmias
Steady-state plasma levels were reached only after several weeks due to slow accumulation
Currently: do not administer; the product has been withdrawn from the market
moa: Selective, long-acting antagonism of peripheral histamine H1 receptors with little CNS penetration (hence non-sedating). Independently of antihistamine action, astemizole and its metabolite block cardiac potassium channels (IKr / hERG), delaying repolarization, prolonging the QT interval and predisposing to torsades de pointes.

absolute: Known QT prolongation or congenital long QT syndrome
Concurrent CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, erythromycin, clarithromycin, ritonavir, nefazodone)
Concurrent other QT-prolonging drugs (Class IA/III antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics)

preg: Not recommended; safety in pregnancy not established and the agent has been withdrawn. Avoid use.
lact: Excreted in breast milk; breastfeeding not recommended during use. Avoid.
renal: Limited specific data; cautious use was advised. Clinically irrelevant now as the drug is withdrawn.
hepatic: Avoid/contraindicated - astemizole is extensively metabolized by CYP3A4 in the liver; impaired hepatic clearance increases plasma levels and the risk of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.

major: CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, erythromycin, clarithromycin, ritonavir, nefazodone) - raise astemizole levels and cause life-threatening QT prolongation / torsades de pointes
Other QT-prolonging drugs (quinidine, procainamide, sotalol, amiodarone, certain antipsychotics, tricyclics) - additive arrhythmia risk
Grapefruit juice - inhibits CYP3A4 and increases astemizole exposure
moderate: Drugs causing electrolyte depletion (potassium-wasting diuretics) - hypokalemia potentiates QT effects
minor: CNS depressants (limited additive sedation given low CNS penetration)
interactions.food: Food reduces bioavailability; grapefruit juice dangerously increases levels via CYP3A4 inhibition.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; product withdrawn and combination offers no benefit.
interactions.diagnostics: QT/QTc prolongation on ECG is the key cardiotoxic signal; monitor potassium and magnesium.

emergency: Torsades de pointes / polymorphic ventricular tachycardia

monitoring: ECG / QTc interval (the reason for withdrawal)
Signs of arrhythmia: palpitations, dizziness, syncope
Concomitant CYP3A4 inhibitors or QT-prolonging drugs
counsel: This medication has been withdrawn worldwide because of serious heart rhythm problems and should not be taken
Never exceed the prescribed dose - higher doses caused fatal arrhythmias
Avoid grapefruit juice and certain antibiotics/antifungals that dangerously raise blood levels
Report any fainting, palpitations, or irregular heartbeat immediately
Ask your clinician about safer modern antihistamine alternatives
pk: Slow; antihistamine effect over hours to days, full effect after weeks
Plasma peak ~1 h (parent); active metabolite accumulates over weeks
Parent ~1-2 days; active metabolite (desmethylastemizole) up to ~9-12 days
Long-acting (>24 h); prolonged due to active metabolite
Store at controlled room temperature (historical product)
pearls: WITHDRAWN worldwide and not an FDA-approved option in current practice - US marketing discontinued (around 1999) and withdrawn across the EU and other regions due to cardiotoxicity
Classic cause of drug-induced QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, especially with CYP3A4 inhibitors, in overdose, or in hepatic impairment
A landmark example, alongside terfenadine and cisapride, that prompted regulatory focus on hERG/QT screening of new drugs
Should not be used; prescribe a safer second-generation antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) instead
Cardiotoxicity is largely independent of its antihistamine action (direct hERG/IKr potassium-channel block)
missed: Not applicable - the drug is withdrawn and should not be in use. (Historically: take the missed dose when remembered, skip if near the next dose, and never double up given the cardiotoxic risk.)
overdose: Overdose causes marked QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiac arrest and death. Management: continuous ECG monitoring for at least 24 hours (longer given the long half-life), correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia, IV magnesium for torsades, consider activated charcoal if recent ingestion, and provide cardiac/supportive care. Avoid further QT-prolonging agents. Dialysis is not expected to be effective (high protein binding).
